questions.prompt: Each thread does C = 4 cycles of compute per load, and memory latency is L = 36 cycles. How many threads does one execution unit need to stay fully busy?
Same C = 4, L = 36, but with only 6 threads. What utilization does the unit reach? Answer as a percentage.
Why can a GPU switch between threads every cycle at essentially no cost?
options: It saves registers to memory very quickly
All resident threads keep their registers on-chip simultaneously, so switching is just choosing which one issues
questions.explanation: Switching is a selection decision, not a save and restore. That's why the register file is so large and why it limits how many threads fit.

questions.prompt: Latency hiding with many threads does what to the latency of each individual load?
options: Leaves it unchanged; other work fills the wait
questions.explanation: Each load takes just as long. The unit simply has other ready work while it waits.

questions.prompt: An SM has 65,536 32-bit registers. If a kernel uses 80 registers per thread, how many threads can be resident (ignoring all other limits and allocation granularity)?
questions.explanation: 65,536 / 80 = 819.2, so 819 threads. Real hardware allocates registers per warp in chunks and schedules whole blocks, so the true number is lower and depends on block size (for example 768 with 256-thread blocks). Part 2 covers this.

questions.prompt: Which changes reduce the number of threads needed to keep an execution unit busy?
options: Issuing several independent loads per thread before using any of them
questions.explanation: More work per load and lower latency shrink (C+L)/C. Independent loads (ILP) give each thread several things in flight. More registers per thread doesn't change the requirement; it reduces how many threads fit.
